newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: South Koreans sceptical over Pyongyang apology.
newsitem.headline: South Koreans sceptical over Pyongyang apology.

text.p: North Korea's apology on Sunday over a submarine incursion could be a desperate gambit to secure food aid and possibly official recognition from the United States, South Korean analysts said.
Some analysts saw it as a grudging response to U.S. badgering, and few believed it was sincere or would lead to dialogue between the rival Koreas any time soon.

Even though it was the first time Pyongyang has officialy apologised over outrages directed against the South, it was a low-cost gesture, the analysts argued. Ordinary North Koreans would never hear it.
The apology was broadcast over Pyongyang radio and the Korean Central News Agency, which are for overseas consumption only.
A good judge of North Korea's sincerity would be whether it dropped its barrage of anti-South Korean propaganda blasted out daily by state media, the analysts said.
"It doesn't look too good," said Rhee Sang-woo, a political science professor at Sogang University and one of South Korea's leading experts on the North.

"North Korea has excluded South Korea and worked the apology out with the U.S. We have won on the content, but lost in the format. North Korea has succeeded in defying the South's sovereignity," he said.
North Korea's unswerving strategy has been to drive a wedge between Seoul and Washington.
Pyongyang wants diplomatic relations with the United States and a bilateral peace accord with Washington to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
Yoo Dong-ryul, a researcher at the Strategy Institute to Counter North Korea, said Pyongyang was only apologising "to overcome its economic crisis and receive western aid, mainly aid from the U.S."

North Korea is on the verge of famine. International food aid has dried up since the submarine intruded in September, sparking world anger. Of 26 North Koreans who landed from the submarine, 24 were shot dead, one was captured alive and one is still on the loose.

"North Korea has been playing tug-a-war with the U.S. for some time now, and has finally given in to the U.S. requests," said Yoo, whose government think-tank is known for its anti-communist hawkishness.
Yoo said he believed the United States had offered a "nice package" to secure the deal, possibly including official recognition for the North Korean government led by Kim Jong-il.
An editorial in the Joong-ang Ilbo newspaper said the apology "would take intra-Korean relations back to September before the submarine incursion, but no further".
The text of the apology was leaked to some South Korean media organisations on Saturday.
Some analysts said that while the apology was not altogether sincere, it was a useful start.
"I guess we are accepting a semi-apology. I think it is positive," said Lee Doo-won, professor of economics at Seoul's Yonsei University.
He urged large South Korean corporations, including the Daewoo Group, to press ahead with North Korean investment plans if the Seoul government relaxes its freeze on cross-border contacts.

"There's no gain to any of the players if we keep the ban on doing business in North Korea. And although a couple of billion dollars for South Korea is not a great deal of money, for the North it is monumental," Lee said.
"We should accept the apology at face value and not get too excited over it."
Yoo said the apology did not indicate North Korea was ready to sit down for talks with the South.
The United States and South Korea have proposed four-way peace talks with the North and China on a peace agreement to replace a truce that ended the 1950-53 Korean War.
"We must not confuse this apology as North Korea opening talks with the South. It was a deal between the North and the U.S.," said Yoo.

Although the apology appeared to satisfy the Seoul governent -- which welcomed it as a chance to "wrap up the submarine incident" -- analysts said it was hard to predict how President Kim Young-sam would respond.
Kim has often been accused by critics of tailoring his North Korea policy to suit the public mood, which has turned viciously anti-Pyongyang since the submarine incident.
"Kim Young-sam doesn't have a plan for North Korea," said Rhee. "If the media says we need to be tougher against the North, he will be tough. If they say the apology is sufficient he will accept it.
"It is like a blind man walking with a stick."
